surface: chessful — /apps/chessful/ (Persuade) + /apps/chessful/privacy/, /apps/chessful/support/ and the six /alternatives/ pages that target it (chess-com, chessable, chessis, chessly, lichess, magnus-trainer) as Read variants

dossier.mechanism: Chessful runs Stockfish on the device over every game you play against its 40 distinct AI opponents. It sorts each significant mistake into one of about thirty named motifs under five skill dimensions (tactics, defense, positional play, openings, endgames) and states it in one or two plain sentences instead of a centipawn line. It then turns those same motifs into tomorrow's spaced-repetition training, offline and with no account.
dossier.audienceScene: An adult club-level player (roughly 800–1800) who knows the rules and keeps losing without knowing why. Most arrive on a phone in the evening, straight after a lost online game, from Google or an AI answer ('chess app that explains mistakes', 'chess training app iphone', 'Chess.com analysis alternative offline', 'Chessis alternative'). Desktop visitors are comparing apps and need to get the app onto an iPhone, iPad or Mac.
dossier.culturalHome: Chess-improvement culture: annotated-game books (Chernev's Logical Chess: Move by Move and the 'Move by Move' tradition); Informant-style figurine notation and its language-free signs (!, ?, !?, ±, □, △); the club night with its roll-up vinyl board, plastic Staunton set, carbon-copy scoresheet and the post-mortem; the Soviet school of training from your own games (Dvoretsky's card file of positions); and the dedicated chess computers of the 1980s. Today the audience lives in Chess.com/Lichess eval-bar culture, which does not serve them. The developer adds one more thread: his grandfather was a chess teacher in the Soviet Union, and the annotation voice is calibrated on him (journal: forty-chess-opponents).
dossier.mustProve: In the first viewport: one real kind of mistake explained as a sentence ('You played Nxd5. The knight was your only back-rank defender.', example_insights 1), set beside what the engine alone shows ('+3.8 → −8.1', how_it_works step 3). The working App Store badge, the desktop QR and the price statement 'Free — Premium from $4.99/mo' are also in view, along with 'iPhone, iPad and Mac · offline · no account'.
dossier.categoryDefault: A dark navy/black page with a glowing gold knight (the app icon's register), a 3D wooden board in an iPhone bezel beside the headline, an accuracy ring or eval bar, a feature-card grid, a pricing table and an FAQ accordion. The other default is the Chess.com green-and-white platform look.
dossier.predictableOpposite: A bright, flat 'learn chess' page with a cartoon mascot and gamified streaks (the Duolingo register), or a clinical white 'AI coach' SaaS page full of accuracy charts and centipawn graphs. That second one is the very thing Chessful says does not teach.
dossier.literalReading: 'Chess-ful' read literally gives a page full of chess sets: board and pieces, wood and gold, and the icon's circuit-traced knight ('AI chess'). Candidate 7 (the Bauhaus chess set, a page built from pieces) is the one literal slot. It was not dealt.

how_it_works step 3 holds the page's proof line verbatim. The engine shows '+3.8 → −8.1, line: Nxd5 Qxe1+ Kh2 Qe5+ g3 Qxd5'; Chessful says 'You played Nxd5 — your knight was the only defender of the back rank, and Black's queen took mate in two'.

App UI (screenshots 1–6): navy ground (~#0B0F1A) and slate cards. Mustard-gold primary buttons ('Train This Pattern', 'Play vs Pebble'). Red 'You played' and green 'Best was' dots, a wood board, figurine move text ('♕b3') and move data in mono ('Move 12. Qb3'). Opponents are listed with ELO and style (Pebble 400 Balanced, Daisy 430 Aggressive, Milo 470 Defensive, Sparky 510 Tactical, Luna 550 Balanced; Robin 580, Otto 610, Ivy 640, Rex …) in tiers of five ('Novice 5/5', 'Beginner 5/5'). Icon: black faceted knight with gold circuit traces on near-black.

_data/testimonials.yml: two real Reddit quotes (S.: 'I get to understand both the mistakes and the engine now'; V.V.), tier hero. Ratings count 11, so no stars appear anywhere.

Journal: forty-chess-opponents (founder's grandfather, a Soviet chess teacher, 'the voice in Chessful's annotations is … more or less his'). 30-chess-mistake-motifs: 30 motifs in 5 dimensions (tactics 10, defense 5, positional 5, openings 3, endgames 7). how-chessful-builds-adaptive-training: 5 stages, 13-ply at club level, rules not a learned classifier.

candidates.name: Annotated-games book (Chernev's Logical Chess: Move by Move, 1957, and the 'Move by Move' tradition)
candidates.why: Every stuck club player is told to read the book that explains each move of a master game in plain words, and that is Chessful's promise applied to your own games. It carries the mechanism as book furniture: your move in bold figurine notation with its '?', one sentence of annotation, a hatched diagram at the turning point, and end-of-chapter exercises drawn from your losses (the training queue) with the solutions at the back.

candidates.name: Club night and the post-mortem (roll-up vinyl board, plastic Staunton set, carbon-copy scoresheet)
candidates.family: club equipment / vinyl, paper form and ritual
candidates.why: Over-the-board chess is really played on a green-and-buff vinyl roll-up board with a duplicate scoresheet, not on wood and gold. The post-mortem (both players replaying the game at the board after the result) is what Chessful does alone with you. It carries the mechanism as your scoresheet: the mistake rows are circled and explained in the margin, then played back on the vinyl board.

candidates.name: Trainer's card file (Dvoretsky's position card index; the Leitner box)
candidates.why: Soviet-school trainers built training from a student's own games and kept the positions on index cards, and the Leitner box is spaced repetition as a physical object. It carries the mechanism literally: each mistake becomes a card filed behind one of five dimension tabs, and the card moves forward through the box until you solve it twice.

candidates.name: Chess Informant's Key to Symbols (Šahovski Informator, Belgrade, from 1966)
candidates.why: Every club player half-knows !, ?, !?, ± and □ from Informant-style annotation, a system built so that nobody needed words. It carries the mechanism by inversion: each sign is followed by the sentence it never said, so the signs become the navigation and the plain sentences become the product.

candidates.name: School report card with the teacher's written remarks
candidates.why: Everyone knows the gap between a grade and the teacher's remark beside it. Chessful's founder line ('a teacher, not a centipawn graph') and the grandfather who taught chess live in that gap. It carries the five skill dimensions as subjects, each with a remark taken from a worked example, and 'homework' as tomorrow's session, though it risks talking down to adults.

candidates.name: 1980s sensory chess computer (Fidelity Chess Challenger, Mephisto, Novag, Saitek)
candidates.why: This was the pre-web offline engine: bought once, no network, an LED lit on the from- and to-squares, LEVEL chosen by pressing a square, and it could never say why. It carries the mechanism as an interface. The board lights your move red and the better one green, the readout gives the reason in a sentence, and LEVEL puts 40 different opponents on 40 squares instead of one engine at 64 settings.

candidates.name: Bauhaus chess set (Josef Hartwig, 1923–24; Joost Schmidt's poster)
candidates.why: Design-minded players know Hartwig's set, where each piece's shape diagrams how it moves (the bishop an X, the rook a cube). It carries 'make the game legible' as geometric motif diagrams, such as a fork drawn as one shape striking two. It is the literal slot (a page built from chess pieces).

styles.label: The Sensory Board
styles.lineage: The dedicated chess computers of 1977–1990: Fidelity Electronics' Chess Challenger (1977, the first commercial unit) and its Sensory boards, Hegener + Glaser's Mephisto, Novag and SciSys/Saitek. They had a printed playing surface with an LED at each square that lit the from- and to-square of the machine's move. They also had a strip of membrane keys (NEW GAME, LEVEL, TAKE BACK, HINT, VERIFY, INFO), a small LCD readout, a level picked on many models by pressing a square, and a printed level table in the manual. The offline engine you bought once, and it never told you why.
styles.thesis: The page is the offline chess machine rebuilt to do what it never could. The board lights the move you played and the better one, the readout says why in a sentence, and LEVEL picks one of 40 different players by square instead of one engine at 64 settings. It refuses the phone-in-a-bezel split hero and the dark eval-graph dashboard.

styles.navigation: The six membrane keys are the microsite nav: NEW GAME (#pricing, red cap), LEVEL (#opponents), TAKE BACK (#templates), HINT (#how-it-works), VERIFY (#privacy), INFO (#quick-reference and #faq). Each key carries a plain sub-legend ('LEVEL · 40 opponents'). The active section's key shows a lit red LED dot. Past the hero the key strip pins to the top with the badge. On mobile, KEYS opens a <details> 2×3 key grid.
styles.signatureInteraction: Level by Square. The LEVEL board is a CSS grid of 64 <a> squares, with the 40 opponents on a1–h5 and ranks 6–8 printed blank. Tapping or arrow-keying to a square (roving tabindex, Enter to select) lights its LED and writes 'PEBBLE · 400 · BALANCED' to the LCD through an aria-live polite region, and the matching level-table row is marked. Without JS, each square is a plain link to its row in the fully visible level table, and the LCD server-renders the first opponent. Under reduced motion the LED switches instantly with no fade or blink.
styles.motionGrammar: Only LEDs move. A lit LED fades in over 120ms as the previous one goes out. HINT blinks the green pair twice (2×300ms), the way a real unit shows its move, then holds steady. Membrane keys press in 1px on :active. No scroll reveals, parallax or sliding panels. prefers-reduced-motion gives instant states with no blink.
styles.readModeVariant: Privacy, support and alternatives are the unit's printed manual. The graphite key strip is the masthead (brand plate, six keys linking back to the microsite, badge right), housing grey is the frame, and the reading column is a #EEEFEA plate 68ch wide in Red Hat Text 17/28 graphite with Saira 700 headings. Privacy opens with the VERIFY LED panel (transparency facts), then the policy text. Support is the 'Service' page: the email in Saira 700 24px, response time, what to include, and the maker's plate. Alternatives print 'Chessful or Chess.com' on the housing. The comparison runs as a spec table on the plate, 'Pick Chessful if… / Stay with Chess.com if…' become the Suitable / Not suitable boxes, then Q & A, with a module well and badge at the foot.
styles.assetsNeeded: (1) The full 40-opponent roster exported from the app (name, ELO, style, tier). Screenshots show only nine names and tiers of five; the a1–h5 layout assumes 8 tiers × 5, and if that is wrong the opponents go in rating order. (2) Six illustrative positions (FEN) authored for the six example_insights, engine-checked and labelled 'illustrative position'. (3) An open-licence SVG piece set (e.g. cburnett, CC BY-SA 3.0, credited in the footer). Everything else (icon, screenshots, QR, badge) exists.
styles.risk: Retro hardware can tip into nostalgia cosplay or a toy look. It has to stay matte, quiet and functional, with the board doing real work. The board-plus-control-panel arrangement must read as one instrument (one housing, keys, wells), not as copy-left/product-right. The chess computer is exactly the 'one engine at levels' that Chessful argues against, so the copy must make that the point and never imply a slider. Younger players may not know the machine, though lit squares and labelled keys read without the reference. Red and green are never the only cue: 'you played' and 'best was' are always printed. A wrong position or roster detail is a visible factual error.
styles.memoryTest: A grey chess-computer page. The board lit red on my mistake and green on the better move, a little display told me why in one sentence, and pressing LEVEL let me pick one of forty named opponents by square.

styles.label: Move by Move
styles.lineage: The annotated-games book: Irving Chernev's Logical Chess: Move by Move (1957), which explains every move of 33 master games in plain words, and the tradition it started (Everyman's 'Move by Move' series, the club-library game collection). Its furniture is a contents page, 'who this book is for', a preface, games headed by players and opening, bold figurine moves each followed by a sentence, printed diagrams with diagonally hatched dark squares and a side-to-move mark, a frontispiece facing the title page, chapter exercises with solutions at the back, and a colophon.
styles.thesis: The page is the chess book every stuck club player is told to read, written about your own games. Your move is in bold with its '?', one sentence explains it, a hatched diagram shows the turning point, and the exercises are built from your losses with the solutions at the back. It refuses the dark-navy app-landing hero and the centipawn-graph analysis page.
styles.scene: A club player on the morning commute, reading on the phone in daylight the way they would read a chess book on the train: white paper, black ink, one green marking pen → light.

styles.navigation: A real contents page is the nav. The verso running head carries 'Contents', which opens a <details> list of chapters (works without JS). styles.signatureInteraction: Play through. Every bold move in an annotation is a button bound to its diagram. Tap '♘xd5?' to see the position after your move with the played squares outlined, and tap 'Better was ♗f4' to switch to the improvement with the green ring (aria-pressed on the move buttons). Each diagram server-renders both positions as static <table> boards. JS shows one at a time and swaps on tap. Without JS, both print side by side at half size, captioned 'After your move' and 'After the better move'. Under reduced motion the swap is instant with no crossfade.
styles.motionGrammar: Paper barely moves. Diagram swaps crossfade over 160ms, and the sticky running-head strip slides 52px in over 180ms. No scroll reveals, parallax or animated numbers. prefers-reduced-motion makes everything instant.
styles.readModeVariant: These pages are chapters of the same book. The running-head nav and paper ground carry over as a single page, not a spread, with a 66ch column in Literata 18/30 ink and the chapter title at opsz 60 wght 650. styles.assetsNeeded: (1) Six illustrative positions (FEN), each with the after-mistake and after-better-move position, for the six example_insights, engine-checked and labelled. (2) An open-licence SVG piece set for diagrams and inline figurines (e.g. cburnett, CC BY-SA 3.0, credited in the colophon). (3) Optional: the 40-opponent roster for the Index of opponents. Otherwise it runs on existing assets.
styles.risk: This is the most familiar of the three. A bookish serif page sits next to the editorial-serif cluster that AI pages fall into. It is the pick because the annotated book is literally the lineage of Chessful's promise, and it escapes the cluster only by being a chess book rather than a magazine: hatched diagrams, bold figurine moves, a contents page and running heads, white not cream, no italic display, no tracked labels. The spread must collapse to one honest page on phones, never a narrow column with fake page edges. The frontispiece facing the title page must read as a book spread, not copy-and-product. A wrong diagram will be spotted by players. Literata's 110 KB leaves no room for a second face.
styles.memoryTest: It read like a chess book about my own games. There was a hatched diagram, my move in bold with a question mark, and one plain sentence telling me what I'd missed. The App Store button sat where a publisher's name goes on a title page.

styles.label: Key to Symbols
styles.lineage: Chess Informant (Šahovski Informator, Belgrade, from 1966) published master games annotated without words, in figurine algebraic notation and a language-independent sign system. The signs include ! good move, ? mistake, ?? blunder, !? interesting, ?! dubious, □ only move, △ with the idea, ± clear advantage, +− winning, ∞ unclear, ⌓ weak point, → attack, ⇆ counterplay and N novelty. Each volume explains them once, at the front, in a multilingual 'Key to symbols' table.
styles.thesis: Chess's most famous annotation system was built to need no words, and Chessful's whole point is the words. The page is set as one long key to symbols: every sign a reader half-knows, followed by the sentence it never said, so the signs are the navigation and the sentences are the product. It refuses the board-in-a-phone hero and the eval-graph dashboard, and there is no board in the first viewport at all.
styles.scene: Late evening on the sofa, the lost game still open on the phone in a dark room. The page arrives as a saturated cobalt field with paper-white signs → dark (color-scheme: dark).

type.rationale: The page argues that notation is the machine and sentences are the teacher, and the type says the same. One variable grotesk spans the key's two jobs: expanded black for signs that read at a glance, condensed for dense key columns, the way a reference periodical's one sans runs both cover and key. Anybody's sturdy, slightly ink-trapped forms keep their character at 220px. A calm transitional book serif carries every sentence Chessful speaks. Total ≈108 KB.

styles.navigation: The key is the nav. The masthead lists signs with their words ('? Mistakes', '△ Method', '⌓ Training', '± Compared', 'Price', '∞ Questions') as plain links, and the active row's sign is underlined 2px paper. On mobile the 'Key' button opens a <details> list of every row (sign + word + anchor), the literal key to the page. Signs always carry their word, never a sign alone.
styles.signatureInteraction: Symbols / Sentences. A masthead toggle (aria-pressed, inserted by JS) sets data-mode='notation' on <html>. The whole page then collapses into pure annotation: moves, signs and the engine line only (e.g. '♗d3? (♕d2!)', '+3.8 → −8.1'), with every sentence hidden. Pressing again brings the words back, so the visitor feels exactly what Chessful adds. Words is the default, and crawlers always get both. Without JS there is no toggle: each row prints the sentence large with its notation line small beneath it. Under reduced motion the swap is instant with no crossfade or height animation.
styles.motionGrammar: Typographic only. Signs never animate. On toggle, sentences and notation crossfade over 140ms and rows change height without animation. Signs hold their place as long rows scroll past (CSS sticky, no JS). No reveals, parallax or counters. prefers-reduced-motion makes everything instant.
styles.readModeVariant: Cobalt stays the frame: the masthead with sign nav, and the page title in Anybody wdth 80 wght 800 on cobalt. The reading column is a paper key page (#F6F5F0, ink #101536) at 66ch in Source Serif 4 18/30. On desktop the sign column persists as the margin. Privacy has '0' beside the transparency table, then the policy text. Support has 'Write' beside the email (Anybody 700 26px), the response time and what to include. Alternatives use '±' beside the comparison table, '!?' and '?!' beside 'Choose Chessful if… / Stay with Chess.com if…', '∞' beside the FAQ, and the install row at the foot. On mobile the sign column shrinks to 56px with signs at row starts.
styles.assetsNeeded: (1) A small SVG set for the non-ASCII signs (□ △ ± ∓ ⌓ ∞ → ⇆), drawn to Anybody Black's stroke weight (~1 KB each). (2) Inline SVG figurines from an open-licence piece set (e.g. cburnett, credited). (3) Optional: the 40-opponent roster for the '40' row. No diagrams are needed. Screenshots, icon, QR and badge exist.
styles.risk: It relies on chess-literate wit. Visitors who have never seen annotation signs must still get it instantly, so every sign always carries its word. A cobalt drench is loud for a calm brand, and it may read 'fintech blue' to anyone without the signs, so long reading happens only on paper panels. Signs used as section markers can slide into decoration, so each must keep its real chess meaning (? mistakes, △ with the idea, ⌓ weak point, N novelty, ∞ unclear, !? worth a try, ?! dubious). Having no board above the fold is a bold bet in a category where visitors expect one, so the screenshots must carry the visual proof. The toggle could be mistaken for a language switch, so it is labelled plainly.
styles.memoryTest: A bright blue page with a giant question mark next to 'Stop guessing' and an exclamation mark next to 'Start understanding'. Every section was marked with a chess annotation sign, and a switch turned the whole page into symbols and back into plain sentences.

canon: Category standard played straight: a dark navy page with the glowing gold circuit-knight icon, a 3D wooden board in an iPhone bezel beside 'Stop guessing. Start understanding.', a badge row, an accuracy ring, a grid of feature cards, a pricing table and an FAQ accordion.
notes: The roll ran degraded (no catalog challengers, no quality-bar boards), as expected; the network was not retried. Seed a17c58e0 assigned 6, which maps to A, THE ROLL (1980s sensory chess computer). Re-roll 1 gave 4, which maps to C, SECOND ROLL (Informant key to symbols). Neither is 1, so B is my top-ranked candidate 1 (annotated-games book) as IMPECCABLE’S PICK, and its risk line names its familiarity. The candidate order was fixed before the roll. The seven span seven material families, and the one literal slot (7, Bauhaus set) was not dealt. Sibling check: Shogiful took the ōban demonstration board with sticky magnet replay, the club tag wall and the manga chapter. Chessful avoids the sticky scrollytelling board: A uses keyed squares, B per-diagram move buttons, and C has no board above the fold. No faces are shared with sibling picks (Atkinson, Barlow, Dela Gothic, Signika, Archivo and others are avoided). Font budgets checked against Fontsource latin files: A ≈133 KB (Saira variable 99 + Red Hat Text 400/600 29 + Doto 700 4), B ≈110 KB (Literata opsz+wght roman), C ≈108 KB (Anybody wdth+wght 57 + Source Serif 4 wght 51). Contrast checked: every text pair is ≥4.5:1, and the LED greens rely on a graphite ring for 3:1. Truth flags for the owner: (1) /alternatives/chess-com/ says Chessful already imports PGN, calls it 'analysis-only' and mentions 'optional iCloud sync'. The app page says PGN import is targeted for 2026 Q3 and that the app ships 40 opponents. Read variants must carry the app page's truth, so that copy needs fixing. (2) The roadmap's 'Targeted 2026 Q3' PGN item has passed (today 2026-10-05; last reviewed 2026-05-13). (3) The forty-chess-opponents post says Premium unlocks 'the full forty-opponent roster', but plans put all 40 in Free. (4) The privacy policy names Game Center leaderboards while the FAQ says 'no leaderboards' (screenshot 5 shows Achievements). (5) Screenshot 3 shows 'Best was ♕a3' for a queen that went d1→b3, and a3 is not reachable from d1, so do not transcribe it as a worked example. (6) Only nine opponents are visible (tiers of five). A's Level by Square needs the full roster export, and the 8×5 layout must be confirmed. (7) All diagram positions are illustrative and must be authored, engine-checked and labelled. (8) The founder signal '19 live apps' is a literal and must stay in sync, while new copy computes the count. (9) alternatives_to lists Really Bad Chess, which has no page. (10) Ratings count is 11, so no stars appear anywhere. The two Reddit quotes in testimonials.yml are real and attributed.
